# Prevalence and Pathologic Characterization of Mouse Kidney Parvovirus in Sentinel CD1 Mice

Zhongming Ge, PhD,1,* Yan Feng, MD,1 Nicola M Parry, MS, BVS, DACVP,2 Damodaran Annamalai, BVS, MVS, PhD, DACLAM,3 Sebastian E Carrasco, DVM, MPVM, MS, PhD, DACVP,4 Melody Guo, SB,1 Sureshkumar Muthupalani, DVM, PhD, DACVP,5 Susan E Erdman, DVM, MPH, DACLAM,1 and James G Fox, DVM, MS, DACLAM1,*

Mouse kidney parvovirus (MKPV) infection can cause significant morbidity and mortality by inducing moderate to severe inclusion body nephropathy and kidney fibrosis in aged immunodeficient mice. However, MKPV infection in immunocompetent mice is associated with histopathologic findings ranging from absent to minimal or moderate lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis without inclusion body in most cases. We surveyed the prevalence of MKPV via PCR from August 2019 through January 2021, using feces, kidneys, and livers collected and pooled from 2 sentinel mice [Crl:CD1(ICR)] (CD1) per surveillance cage (a total of 212 cages). CD1 mice used as dirty-bedding sentinels were housed for 6 mo in a separate cage on the same rack as colony mice used in research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research. MKPV quantitative PCR positivity was 16.04%, 14.62%, and 10.02% for feces, kidney, and liver, respectively. The aggregate prevalence of MKPV was 22.64% (48 of 212 samples). Thirty-three of 103 rooms (32.04%) were MKPV positive. MKPV-positive kidneys had more severe chronic lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis (CLIN) than MKPV-negative kidneys; however, there was no significant difference in hepatic lesions between MKPV-positive and -negative livers. Although no overt intranuclear inclusion body nephropathy was noted in MKPV-positive CD1 kidneys, MKPV RNA was sporadically detected within tubular epithelial cells in MKPV-positive kidneys but not in MKPV-positive livers. Our study indicates that MKPV can be easily transmitted through soiled bedding. It highlights that CD1 mice can be used as sentinels to detect MKPV, emphasizing the importance of monitoring MKPV distribution using quantitative PCR in sentinel mice if MKPV needs to be excluded from a colony. Importantly, as MKPV infection is associated with mild to moderate CLIN, MKPV can potentially confound the interpretation of in vivo biomedical data.

Introduction Mouse kidney parvovirus (MKPV) is widespread in laboratory research colonies.3,5,7,11 MKPV, which is phylogenetically divergent from previously known mouse parvoviruses (for example, mouse parvovirus-1 and minute virus of mice) that also infect laboratory mice, is a member of the virus species Rodent chaphamaparvovirus 1 in the genus Chaphamaparvovirus of the newly established subfamily Hamaparvovirinae.9,11,14 The evidence clearly demonstrates that MKPV infection can induce inclusion body nephropathy (IBN) and kidney fibrosis in severely immunocompromised laboratory mouse strains, including NSG (NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ), B6.129P2-Cxcr6tm1Lit-tRag1tm1Mom/J, B6.Cg-Rag1tm1MomTyrp1B-wTg (Tcra, Tcrb)9Rest/M, and B6.Cg- Il2rg-/-Rag2-/-KitW-sh/ HNihrJaeBsmGlliJ.5,7,10-12 In addition, it has been reported that MKPV infection is linked to the development of lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis in immunocompetent mice, including experimentally infected C57BL/6 mice, naturally infected Swiss

Webster and outbred Crl:CD1(ICR) (CD1) mice.3,10,11 Furthermore, a closely related virus, namely murine chapparvovirus (MuCPV), was identified in wild Mus musculus mice collected from the urban areas of New York City, and a similar virus is globally distributed in wild and laboratory mice.7,11,14 Finally, a recent study reported that in the adenine B6 model of chronic kidney disease, MKPV-infected mice had more interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltration (at 4 and 8 wk of adenine diet consumption) and less interstitial fibrosis (at 8 wk) compared with uninfected mice, emphasizing MKPV infection as a potential confounding factor in mouse models of renal diseases.10

A causal relationship between MKPV and IBN in immunocompromised mice has been established by studies that have demonstrated MKPV transmission in cohoused mice, with a correlation between virus abundance and severity of IBN that has satisfied the Fredrick and Relman criteria.4,5,7,11 However, a similar causal relationship between MKPV and IBN has not fully corroborated in immunocompetent mice, although some features of MKPV-associated IBN were noted in inbred C57BL/6, outbred CD1 and Swiss Webster mice.3,10,11 Immunocompetent CD1 mice, which are outbred, have been extensively used as all-purpose stocks for research, drug testing, and pathogen surveillance in research animal facilities.2 It has been reported that MKPV was persistently detected in naturally infected CD1 mice up to 10 mo after the initial positive PCR test, whereas the

MKPV in sentinel CD1 mice

MKPV abundance peaked at 10 to 14 wk after both an oral and an intranasal inoculation in urine and feces and then decreased up to 35 wk in CD1 mice experimentally dosed with the viral stocks prepared from a naturally MKPV-infected kidney of an NSG mouse.3,6 Although MKPV positivity and associated renal lesions in sentinel CD1 mice were previously reported, systematic evaluation on viral distribution among feces, liver, and kidney as well as MKPV-associated renal pathology in sentinel CD1 mice housed in our facilities will further strengthen the importance of sentinel CD mice in MKPV surveillance, MKPV diagnosis, and MKPV-associated renal disease and the argument of the potential of confounding impact on research of renal disease. It will also provide an additional compelling justification for monitoring the prevalence of MKPV in mice housed in research animal facilities. Recently, we identified a new strain (MIT-WI1) of MKPV in mice housed at MIT and the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (WI). MIT-WI1 was detected in fecal samples of sentinel CD1 mice cohousing in separate cages on racks in select mouse vivaria.5 In this study, we systematically surveyed the prevalence of MKPV using sentinel CD1 mice originating from the MIT and WI animal facilities and also evaluated histopathologic features associated with MKPV infection in these mice.

Materials and Methods Mouse strains and surveillance program. An in-house MIT breeding supply colony produces female CD1 outbred stock mice used for surveillance purposes. New parental CD1 stocks (MKPV-free CD1 Elite; Charles River Laboratories, Quebec, Canada) arrive once per year and produce offspring used for this sentinel program. After weaning, 4 sentinel CD1 mice were housed in a separate cage on the bottom shelf of one of the holding racks housing mice used in research. Surveillance mice received used bedding consisting of one 30-g scoop of used bedding from all cages in the designated animal room, with bedding collections done on a rotating basis using cages of a single rack per week. The surveillance cages were changed last in a room. The cage bedding was hardwood chip bedding (SottPharma Solutions, Marlborough, MA) with enrichment (Nestlets, Ancare, Bellmore, NY; EnviroPak, FiberCore, Cleveland, OH). Mice also received γ-irradiated feed (LabDiet RMH 3000; Purina Mills International, St. Louis, MO) and filtered or reverse osmosis water ad libitum according to the animal facility. The animal holding room was maintained at 70 ± 2 °F and 30% to 70% relative humidity and a 12:12-h light:dark cycle. Sentinel CD1 mice were placed in 103 rooms of 6 vivaria (V) at MIT and WI.8 Of these tested rooms, 30 (8 in V1 and 22 in V2) were used for housing mice from atypical sources without rederivation, whereas 73 (11 in V3, 12 in V4, 28 in V5, and 22 in V6) were used for housing mice from approved vendors and/or after rederivation. Animals in all CD1 breeding cages were tested twice annually using CRL Pilot Records Improvement Act surveillance-plus PCR testing and were found to be negative for commonly recognized opportunistic pathogens as follows: mouse viral pathogens (mouse hepatitis virus, Sendai virus, MPV, MVM, pneumonia virus of mice, Theiler meningoencephalitis virus GDVII, mouse rotavirus EDIM, ectromelia virus, reovirus type 3, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, K virus, mouse adenovirus 1 and 2, and polyoma virus), bacteria (Mycoplasma pulmonis, Helicobacter spp., Citrobacter rodentium, Salmonella spp., Filobacterium rodentium, Staphylococcus aureus, Beta hemolytic Streptococcus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, all Pasteurella spp., Corynebacterium kutscherii, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella spp., and Bordetella bronchiseptica), ectoparasites (Myobia musculi, Myocoptes musculinis, Polyplax

serrata and Radfordia affinis), and endoparasites (Syphacia spp., Aspicularis spp., Trichuris muris, and Hymenolepsis spp.). The mice were housed under speciﬁc pathogen-free conditions in AAALAC-accredited facilities in static microisolater cages and provided with water ad libitum. All animal housing conditions and experimental protocols were approved by the MIT Committee on Animal Care. Necropsy and tissue sampling. Of 4 CD1 mice in each surveillance cage, 1 mouse was necropsied for diagnostic tests at 2 and 4 mo of sentinel housing, respectively, which was not included in this study. After serving as sentinel mice for approximately 6 mo, 2 CD1 mice from each surveillance cage were euthanized with CO2, and comprehensive necropsies were performed. At necropsy, samples pooled from 2 mice per sentinel cage, including feces (1 to 2 pellets per mouse) from the colon, kidney (one longitudinally sliced half of the left kidney), and/or liver (a sections of each lobe), were collected and stored at –20 °C, before further molecular characterization. For histologic evaluation, transverse sections of the right kidney and the remaining longitudinally sliced half of the left kidney, as well as sections of each liver lobe were placed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin and allowed to fix for at least 48 h, before routine processing and embedding in paraffin. During the period from August 2019 to January 2021, a total of 211 fecal samples (missing from 1 surveillance cage) and 211 kidney samples (missing from another surveillance cage) were collected from 212 surveillance cages, while 137 liver samples from 137 surveillance cages were collected during March 2020 to January 2021. DNA extraction from fresh murine tissues, fecal samples, and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues. Total DNA was extracted from frozen kidneys, livers, and feces of sentinel CD1 mice, using the High Pure PCR Template Preparation Kit (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN) and QIAamp Stool DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues from MKPV-positive C57BL/6 Il2rg-/-Rag2-/-cKitW-sh mice (B6.Il2rRag2W) were used as MKPV-positive controls were sectioned at 15-µm thickness, following a protocol that prevented cross-contamination of MKPV between samples, as described previously.5 The sectioned tissues were deparaffinized, and DNA was prepared using the QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The purity and concentration of the DNA obtained were examined in the Nanodrop 2000C Spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Rockford, IL). MKPV quantitative PCR. MKPV-specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) assay was developed as described previously.5 Briefly, qPCR assays were performed in a 10-µL volume consisting of 5 µL 2X Fast Universal Mixture (ThermoFisher Scientific), 3 µL DNA template, and 1 µL of the probe/primers mixture in the 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR Detection System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the default setting. The genome copies of MKPV in the samples were normalized to micrograms of murine DNA, which was quantified using the 18S rRNA gene-based primers/ probe (ThermoFisher Scientific). Histologic evaluation.  FFPE tissues were sectioned at 5-μm thickness and stained with hematoxylin-eosin. Pathologic changes on the stained slides were graded (by NMP a board-certified veterinary pathologist) as described previously.5 Sections of the kidney were examined at 100 to 200× magnification for features of IBN. These features included tubular lesions (including tubular atrophy or loss; tubular degeneration, regeneration, and necrosis; and karyomegaly and intranuclear inclusion bodies in tubular epithelial

Based on histologic examination, sections of kidney were then graded for IBN using a semiquantitative scale of 0 to 4, in which grading scores (in parenthesis) were assigned according to the percentage of kidney parenchyma affected by IBN lesions: no lesions, 0% (0); minimum to mild, 1% to 3% (0.5), 4% to 6% (1), and 7% to 9% (1.5); mild to moderate, 10% to 17% (2) and 18% to 25% (2.5); moderate to severe, 26% to 50% (3) and 51% to 75% (3.5); and severe, greater than 75% (4). The total number of intranuclear inclusion bodies seen in tubular epithelial cells in 5 random fields at 400 × magnification was also recorded. Kidneys were surveyed for any histologic lesions not typically attributed to IBN (including glomerular lesions, and pyelonephritis). Where present, these were scored by severity, using a semiquantitative scale of 0 to 4, in which grade scores were assigned based on the percentage of kidney parenchyma affected by the lesions in a similar manner to those used for IBN lesions as described above: no lesions, 0% (0); minimum to mild, 1% to 3% (0.5), 4% to 6% (1), and 7% to 9% (1.5); mild to moderate, 10% to 17% (2) and 18% to 25% (2.5); moderate to severe, 26% to 50% (3) and 51% to 75% (3.5); and severe, greater than 75% (4). Kidneys were also surveyed for other miscellaneous lesions (including mineralization, hydronephrosis, and tumor). Kidneys were scored for the presence (1) or absence (0) of any such lesions identified as described previously.5 Sections of liver were examined for any histologic lesions (including hepatocellular degeneration or necrosis, periportal inflammation, parenchymal inflammation, lipidosis, bile duct hyperplasia, lymphoid aggregate formation, and microgranulomas). Where present, these were scored using a semiquantitative scale of 0 to 4, according to lesion severity: 0, no lesions; 1, minimal to mild; 2, mild to moderate; 3, moderate to severe; and 4, diffusely severe as described previously.13 Severity of renal and hepatic pathologic changes were compared between MKPV-positive and -negative mice for statistical significance. Chromogenic in situ hybridization of MKPV RNA. MKPV RNA in kidneys and livers of sentinel CD1 mice with MKPV positivity in both kidney and livers (n = 6) in parallel with MKPV-negative controls (n = 3) and IBN kidneys of MKPV-infected B6.Il2rRag2W (n = 3) was visualized using chromogenic in situ hybridization (fast red chromogen), with a hybridization probe designed to target a sequence of the genome partially covering ns1 and vp1, as described previously.5 The assay was performed in ACD HybEZ II Hybridization System (Advanced Cell Diagnostics [ACD], Newark, CA) using the RNAscope 2.5 HD Reagent Kit-Red, following the ACD protocols. Control probes detecting a validated positive housekeeping gene (mouse peptidylprolyl isomerase B [Ppib] to confirm adequate RNA preservation; 313918; Advanced Cell Diagnostics) and a negative control (Bacillus subtilis dihydrodipicolinate reductase gene [dapB] to confirm the absence of nonspecific labeling; 312038; Advanced Cell Diagnostics) were used. Positive RNA hybridization was identified as punctate chromogenic red dots under bright field microscopy. Statistical analyses. All statistical analyses were performed using the Prism GraphPad 9 Package. Data that were normally distributed (as determined using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) were compared via the unpaired Student t test, and other data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. The χ2 test (2-tailed) was used to analyze MKPV positivity among feces, kidneys, and liver. Linear regression and Pearson

correlation between the abundance of MKPV and severity of IBN were performed. P values of less than 0.05 were considered significant.

Notably, the prevalence of MKPV was significantly lower (P < 0.03) in the rooms housing mice originating from approved commercial vendors or mice with embryo rederivation (19.2%, 14 of 73 rooms/cubicles) compared with the rooms/cubicles housing mice from atypical sources or without rederivation (63.3%, 19 of 30 rooms/cubicles). Chronic lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis was more severe in MKPV-positive kidneys compared with those without MKPV. Next, we examined and compared renal pathology between MKPV-positive and MKPV-negative kidneys of sentinel CD1 mice. Compared with MKPV-negative healthy kidneys (Figure 2A), MKPV-positive kidneys with CLIN were characterized by relatively mild overall changes, comprising one or more of the following lesions with minimal to mild severity (score, 1 to 2): CLIN was the most common finding (Figure 2B and C); less frequently, some renal tubules had variably attenuated or slightly swollen epithelial cells, distended lumina, and occasional luminal protein or cellular debris, but there was no difference in severity between MKPV-positive and -negative CD1 kidneys (data not shown). The overall scores of CLIN were significantly higher in MKPV-positive kidneys

than in MKPV-negative kidneys from MKPV-free or fecal MKPV-positive sentinel CD1 mice (Figure 2D). There was no significant difference in the severity of CLIN between the kidneys from MKPV-negative mice and the kidneys from mice that were solely fecal MKPV positive. Minimal hydronephrosis, tubular lesions, and glomerular lesions (score, less than or equal to 1, data not shown) were noted in some mice, but there was no significant difference between MKPV-positive and MKPV-negative kidneys. In addition, MKPV-affected kidneys of these sentinel CD1 mice from our animal facilities did not develop overt IBN lesions (characterized by multifocal areas of tubular loss, tubular atrophy, tubular necrosis, and degeneration, with karyomegaly and intranuclear inclusions, and interstitial fibrosis) as previously described in severely immunocompromised B6.Il2rRag2W mice.5 There was no significant difference in hepatic lesions between MKPV positive and MKPV negative CD1 mice (data not shown), with typically minimal to mild (score, 1 to 2) changes seen, comprising multiple small foci of hepatocellular necrosis, with or without associated neutrophils. The affected kidneys contained significantly higher levels of MKPV compared with the livers (P = 0.0001) and feces (P < 0.0001), whereas there was no significant difference in MKPV levels between livers and feces (P = 0.436). Furthermore, MKPV RNA in the kidneys and livers of MKPV DNA+ CD1 mice was examined using chromogenic in situ hybridization (ISH). Discussion Our data show that CD1 mice used as sentinels for approximately 6 mo can horizontally acquire MKPV and the viral DNA is persistently present in the kidney and liver, presumably via dirty bedding transfer. MKPV-positive CD1 kidneys developed significantly higher grades of CLIN compared with MKPV-negative kidneys. In addition, there was only sparse MKPV RNA labeling within the tubular cells, and no histologic evidence of inclusion bodies and the MKPV-associated tubular degenerative changes noted in the MKPV-positive sentinel CD1 kidneys. These findings are in stark contrast with the widespread MKPV RNA labeling in the kidneys of B6.Il2rRag2W mice with mild to severe IBN.5 Similarly, one study reported that the MKPV-positive kidneys from naturally infected CD1 and Swiss Webster mice had MKPV RNA labeling within collecting ducts 177 to 198 d after the initial MKPV-positive test. However, differences in the development of MKPV-associated renal pathology were noted between a previous report3 and our study: 1) only the longer naturally MKPV exposure group (318 to 334 d after the initial positive test) developed significantly higher grades of renal pathology ranging from mild to moderate lymphoplasmacytic interstitial nephritis compared with age-matched virus-negative mice, whereas the cohort of CD1 mice in our study took approximately 6 mo or less for such pathologic changes; 2) more severe tubular degeneration was observed in the virus infected kidneys, while no difference in tubular changes between MKPV positive and negative kidneys was observed in the present study; and 3) eosinophilic inclusion bodies with ISH MKPV RNA labeling were observed in one CD1 mouse but were absent from our CD1 mice. In addition, histologic evidence of MKPV intranuclear inclusion bodies associated with moderate tubular degeneration was also described in one sentinel Swiss Webster mouse.11 These differences in the observation of MKPV renal inclusion bodies and tubular changes in CD1 mice can be attributed to multiple factors such as pathogenicity of virus strains, virus infection duration, mouse stocks, husbandry conditions, the difference in histopathology evaluation methods and the hosts’ gut microbiome. A recent study reported that CD1, B6, and NSG mice were experimentally infected with MKPV after both oral and intranasal inoculations with a viral suspension prepared from an MKPV/IBN-affected kidney of an NSG mouse.6 By 35 wk after the virus inoculation, the NSG mice developed overt signs of morbidity due to MKPV-associated IBN, but the MKPV-positive CD1 and B6 mice showed no clinical signs of MKPV-associated renal disease.6 This clinical finding could be at least partially attributed to viral load peaking in CD1 and B6 mice at approximately 12 wk postviral inoculation and decreasing after this time point.6 Experimentally MKPV-infected B6 female mice in another study developed more severe interstitial lymphoplasmacytic nephritis with tubular generation compared with uninfected controls at 14 wk after viral inoculation.10 In addition, intranuclear inclusions were observed in 1 of 23 (4%) MKPV-positive B6 mice.10 Taken together, current data suggest that MKPV infection in immunocompetent mice can be predominantly associated with subclinical renal pathology and that viral load is suppressed probably via limiting viral propagation, immune-regulated clearance, or both. Future investigations are warranted to provide new insights into how aging, immune responses, the host’s microbiome, and MKPV strains influence the pathogenesis of MKPV. MKPV in sentinel CD1 mice

MKPV nucleotide sequences from immunocompetent mouse strains including sentinel CD1, housed in different locations of our facilities, were identical to MKPV MIT-WI1 in the approximately 300-nucleaotide region displaying single nucleotide polymorphism among known MKPV/MuCPV strains.5 These data suggest that there is a single strain of MKPV distributed in mice housed in our facilities. However, the whole genome sequences of MKPV isolates need to be determined to confirm MKPV clonality. In our current retrospective study, we show that MKPV was moderately distributed, as evidenced by a MKPV positivity rate of 22.64% in murine tissues and feces (48 of 211 samples) and MKPV positivity in 32% of the tested rooms (33 of 103 rooms). Notably, the prevalence of MKPV was markedly lower in the vivaria housing rederived mice from atypical sources or mice from approved commercial sources compared with the vivaria housing mice consisting of breeding colonies of various transgenic lines, which had not been rederived via embryo transfer. Although it is unclear how MKPV was introduced into some of the rooms housing the mice with rederivation or from commercial vendors, we speculate that the presence of MKPV was likely attributable to several possible sources: 1) some lines of commercial source mice were not free of MKPV when being introduced into our facility before availability of MKPV PCR screening7,11; 2) MKPV transmitted by application of virus-contaminated biologics; and 3) MKPV transmitted by animal care or research personnel. Nevertheless, these results were consistent with previous reports showing mice rederived from MKPV-positive mouse strains were

MKPV-free via PCR.5,11 Our findings highlight that rederivation, which was used to eradicate Helicobacter spp in mice housed in our animal facilities,8 is also likely effective in eliminating MKPV from the affected mouse colonies. Based on the findings from previous and current studies, a systematic MKPV-qPCR screening protocol via fecal qPCR is currently being discussed for incorporating into our surveillance program to help prevent MKPV infection from being spread among vivaria. We also documented that fecal qPCR was apparently an effective, noninvasive for identifying MKPV positivity in a sentinel setting, with an MKPV positivity rate of 70.83% compared with 64.58% in the kidney. In addition, MKPV positivity from kidney and feces combined accounted for 91% of MKPV-positive CD1 mice. Furthermore, previous studies showed that detectable MKPV levels appeared approximately 2 wk earlier in urine than in feces from CD1 mice after viral inoculation and that there is a strong correlation in MKPV abundance between urine and urine-soaked feces.3,6 Our surveillance protocol supports a similar previously reported surveillance strategy that tested urine-soaked fecal pellets together with swabs, dirty bedding, and renal tissue.3,6 In addition, use of mice from approved commercial vendors certified to be free of MKPV or rederived mice can significantly reduce the risk of introducing MKPV into institutional animal facilities. Finally, it has been demonstrated that MKPV can be effectively eliminated from the contaminated cages after a tunnel wash (88 °C final rinse for 20 s) since CD1 mice in untreated cages became MKPV positive by 20 wk, whereas in contrast all CD1 mice in tunnel wash-treated cages with or without sterilization (120 °C for 20 min) were negative for MKPV.1

Discordance in MKPV positivity was noted among multiple sample types (feces, kidney, and liver) collected from the same mice. This observation is consistent with a prior report in which discordance in MKPV positivity was noted among kidney, bladder, dirty bedding, cage swabs, fecal pellets, and cecal content in some mice.3 This is likely a consequence of MKPV infection dynamics that are modulated by multiple factors, including viral strains, initial infection dosage, stage of infection, and the genetic background of a host. Insufficient MKPV abundance in mice could be a critical factor for site-restricted positivity. This premise is supported by our data showing that renal MKPV levels in solely kidney-positive mice or fecal MKPV levels in solely feces-positive mice were lower by approximately 8,000-fold or by 4-fold, respectively, compared with those in the corresponding samples from mice which were MKPV-positive at both sites. The former was likely due to suppression of MKPV propagation in the kidneys of these individual CD1 mice, whereas the latter may result from the fact that MKPV was being recently introduced into CD1 mice via exposure to dirty bedding from research colonies during the 6 mo of sentinel exposure. The hypothesis of the suppression of MKPV propagation in the kidney is in line with a recent report showing that the shedding of MKPV from CD1 mice was significantly reduced by 12 wk after oral and intranasal inoculation of MKPV.6

We found that 1) MKPV-positive CD1 livers showed no histologically significant lesions; 2) the hepatic MKPV genome copies were significantly lower compared with those in the corresponding kidneys; and 3) MKPV RNA labeling, as examined via chromogenic ISH, was absent from the MKPV DNA+ livers of sentinel CD1 mice. These results are consistent with prior findings in immunodeficient, immunocompetent, and wild-living mice, where MKPV DNA was consistently detected in the liver at a lower level than in the kidney.3,7,11,14 In addition, MKPV RNA labeling was not noted in the livers of naturally infected Rag1-/- mice with IBN or in CD1 mice; it was found only in a single NGS mouse.3,7 Given that expression of MKPV RNA is integral for viral propagation, positive correlation between hepatic and renal MKPV DNA levels suggests that viral propagation dynamics in liver and kidney may be similar in individual mice, although significantly suppressed in the liver compared with the kidney. These lines of evidence suggest that MKPV elicits minimal pathology in liver compared with kidney, possibly due to the limited viral propagation that is attributable to a weak host cell receptor(s) for viral entry. Alternatively, the limited MKPV propagation in murine liver may be a consequence of latent infection during viremia.7 Of note, approximately 4% of MKPV-positive sentinel mice were positive for MKPV only in the liver (2 of 48), which may be a result of transient infection via viremia. Experimental delineation of the mechanisms underlying differences in MKPV pathogenesis between murine liver and kidney will provide new insights into MKPV pathophysiology in mice. Our study has some limitations. All specimens were collected and pooled from 2 CD1 mice per cage at the end of their sentinel residence time (approximately 6 mo), and thus the temporal viral transmission status and MKPV status in the individual CD1 mice housed in the same cage are not known. Earlier time

points to monitor for MKPV infection in surveillance mice should be used. Although our data indicated that sentinel CD1 mice acquired MKPV via exposure to soiled bedding, resident mouse strains from which MKPV originated were not identified. Finally, the MKPV status in the gastrointestinal tract is uncharacterized. These parameters will be included for investigation in a future study. In summary, we demonstrated that CD1 mice can be used as an effective sentinel for determining MKPV status. Our results indicate that qPCR-based tests using fecal pellets, even though a more sensitive but time-consuming strategy of using urine-soaked fecal pellets as proposed previously,3,6 from live surveillance animals provide an effective noninvasive method for detecting MKPV. Given that no single tissue sample identifies all MKPB-positive cases, renal and hepatic tissues from euthanized sentinel mice should be also included in PCR-based MKPV diagnosis to examine the status of MKPV infection.
